extracted.intended_audience: students of mathematical logic / model theory (advanced undergraduate or beginning graduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of core model-theoretic facts in first-order logic (decidability for finite structures, Löwenheim–Skolem theorems, theories and axiomatizability, categoricity tests, prenex normal form, and definitions of functions). Intended as textbook material for learning and applying these results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite structure representability
rubrics_metrics.description: A finite structure for a finite language can be specified by a finite string of symbols (e.g., listing the universe {1,...,n} and the relations/functions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a structure can be communicated to a person or machine and written in a suitable input format (numerals, punctuation, delimiters). This underlies effective procedures that operate on finite structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective evaluation of formulas in a finite structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a finite structure A (universe {1,...,n}), a wff ϕ, and an assignment of numbers to free variables, one can effectively decide whether A |= ϕ[s].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize the computation as a tree: each quantifier triggers a search through the n-element universe; for a formula with k quantifiers the number of leaves is bounded by a polynomial in n of degree k. Atomic formulas at leaves are checked by table look-up. If the language has function symbols, each term must be evaluated using the finite function provided by the structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Th A decidable for finite A in finite language (Theorem 26C)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a finite structure A in a finite language, the theory Th A (set of sentences true in A) is decidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two proofs: (1) Replace A by an isomorphic structure with universe {1,...,n} and apply the effective evaluation procedure. (2) Use a sentence δA that specifies A up to isomorphism; then Th A = {σ | δA |= σ}, and apply enumerability/decidability results (noting for each σ either A |= σ or A |= ¬σ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decidability of 'σ has an n-element model'
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a sentence σ and positive integer n, one can effectively decide whether σ has a model of size n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are only finitely many structures on universe {1,...,n} for the language restricted to parameters appearing in σ; systematically generate and test them using the effective evaluation procedure (observation 3). Example: with a single 2-place predicate there are 2^(n^2) different structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectrum decidability
rubrics_metrics.description: The spectrum of a sentence σ (the set {n | σ has a model of size n}) is a decidable set of positive integers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from the effective decision procedure for 'σ has an n-element model' by checking each n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective enumerability of sentences with finite models (Theorem 26D)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a finite language, the set {σ | σ has a finite model} is effectively enumerable (semidecidable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Semidecision procedure: given σ, check successively for models of size 1, 2, 3, ... using the finite-model decision procedure; halts iff some finite model is found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complement of sentences true in every finite structure is enumerable (Corollary 26E)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let FIN be the set of sentences true in every finite structure. Then FIN^c (the complement) is effectively enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: σ ∈ FIN iff ¬σ has no finite model; thus enumerate sentences for which ¬σ has a finite model using the semidecision procedure of Theorem 26D.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trakhtenbrot's theorem (finite validity undecidable)
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of sentences true in every finite structure is not, in general, decidable or effectively enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows the analogue of enumerability for arbitrary structures fails when restricted to finite structures: finite validities are undecidable in general (no effective complete procedure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Countability of model constructed in completeness proof (size of A/E)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the initial language is countable, the canonical model A/E constructed from a consistent set has countable universe (so a consistent set of sentences in a countable language has a countable model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universe of preliminary A is set of terms in a countable augmented language (countable); quotienting by equivalence classes preserves countability (choose representatives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Löwenheim–Skolem theorem (downward and basic form)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If a set of formulas in a countable language is satisfiable, it has a countable model. (b) If a set of sentences in a countable language has any model, then it has a countable model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via completeness and the countability observation, or by extracting a countable elementary/substructure from any model. Historical notes: versions due to Löwenheim and Skolem; leads to Skolem's paradox for set theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Löwenheim–Skolem theorem (cardinality λ)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a set of formulas is satisfiable in a language of cardinality λ, it is satisfiable in some structure of size ≤ λ; similarly for sets of sentences: if any model exists, a model of size ≤ λ exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction parallels the countable case but with λ many new constants; uses that set of terms has cardinality ≤ λ and quotienting keeps cardinality ≤ λ (may need Choice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Upward Löwenheim–Skolem / LST theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If a set of formulas in a language of cardinality λ has an infinite model, then for every κ ≥ λ there is a model of cardinality κ in which the set is satisfiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expand language by κ many new constant symbols required to be distinct; apply compactness and Löwenheim–Skolem to obtain a model of cardinality κ; then restrict to original language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-categoricity of theories with infinite models
rubrics_metrics.description: If a set of sentences has any infinite models, then it is not categorical (i.e., not all models are isomorphic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary of upward/downward Löwenheim–Skolem: such a theory has models of different infinite cardinalities, so cannot be categorical in all infinite sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory (definition) and Th K
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory is a set of sentences closed under logical implication (T is a theory iff T |= σ ⇒ σ ∈ T). For a class K of structures, Th K = {σ | σ true in every member of K}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Th K is indeed a theory; examples include theory of fields, theory of fields of characteristic 0, and theory of a single structure Th A which is complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and axiomatizability of theories
rubrics_metrics.description: T is complete iff for every sentence σ either σ ∈ T or ¬σ ∈ T. T is axiomatizable iff there is a decidable set Δ with T = Cn(Δ). T is finitely axiomatizable iff Δ can be finite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: an axiomatizable theory is effectively enumerable; a complete axiomatizable theory is decidable (Corollary 26I). Examples: theory of fields axiomatizable; theory of fields characteristic 0 axiomatizable but not finitely axiomatizable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite axiomatizability lemma (Theorem 26H)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Cn(Σ) is finitely axiomatizable then there is finite Σ0 ⊆ Σ with Cn(Σ0) = Cn(Σ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses compactness: if Cn(Σ) = Cn(τ) for some τ, then Σ |= τ so by compactness some finite subset Σ0 |= τ, giving equal consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Łoś–Vaught test for completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Let T be a theory in a countable language with no finite models. If T is ℵ0-categorical then T is complete; more generally if T is κ-categorical for some infinite κ (with language cardinality ≤ κ) then T is complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces models to cardinal κ using LST and then uses isomorphism at cardinal κ to conclude elementary equivalence for arbitrary models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of applying categoricity/completeness (Theorem 26J)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) The theory of algebraically closed fields of characteristic 0 is complete. (b) The theory of the complex field (C;0,1,+,·) is decidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide axioms for algebraically closed fields char 0 (field axioms + sentences asserting solvability of polynomials), note axiomatizable; show κ-categoricity for uncountable κ via algebraic classification (Steinitz) and apply Łoś–Vaught to get completeness and hence decidability for C. Note: theory of reals is decidable (Tarski) but needs deeper methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and decidability for dense linear orders without endpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory δ of dense linear orders without endpoints is ℵ0-categorical (Cantor): any countable model of δ is isomorphic to (Q,<). Hence Cn δ is complete and the theories of (Q,<) and (R,<) are decidable and elementarily equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give axioms: ordering axioms (trichotomy, transitivity), density, no endpoints. Cantor's theorem yields isomorphism of countable models; Łoś–Vaught gives completeness and decidability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prenex normal form theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Every formula is logically equivalent to a prenex formula of the form Q1 x1 ... Qn xn α where Qi ∈ {∀,∃} and α is quantifier-free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quantifier manipulation rules Q1–Q3 (negation swapping ¬∀ ↔ ∃¬, moving quantifiers across implications with freshness conditions, etc.) and induction on formula complexity. Examples show different possible orders of quantifiers may result (latitude in application of rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifier manipulation rules (Q1–Q3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equivalences used to move quantifiers: Q1a ¬∀x α ↔ ∃x ¬α; Q1b ¬∃x α ↔ ∀x ¬α. Q2/Q3 variants for moving quantifiers across implications given freshness conditions (variables not free in certain subformulas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit use in converting formulas with → and ¬ to prenex form; examples illustrate allowed permutations of quantifiers when variables are alphabetic variants and do not clash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of function symbols must be well-defined (noncreative definition criterion, Theorem 27A)
rubrics_metrics.description: When adding a new function symbol f by definition ∀v1 ∀v2[f v1 = v2 ↔ ϕ(v1,v2)], the definition is noncreative (adds no consequences in the smaller language) iff T proves the uniqueness/existence sentence ∀v1 ∃!v2 ϕ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If T |= ∀v1 ∃!v2 ϕ then for any model A of T there is a unique function F mapping each d to the unique e with ϕ[d,e], and (A,F) models the definition δ; conversely δ entails ε = ∀v1 ∃!v2 ϕ, so noncreativity ⇔ well-definedness. Counterexample: definitions that do not ensure uniqueness can produce contradictions (e.g., f(1)=2 and f(1)=3).
